I am fifty-four years old, and I have worked this land in Quzhou since I was a boy. My father taught me how to read the soil with my hands, and forty years of sweat have shown me what these forty-two mu can bear. With five mouths to feed at home, I cannot gamble everything on one crop, so I keep my fields divided the way my neighbors and I have always done: wheat and maize are my backbone, cotton brings in cash when the price is right, and a small plot of cucumber gives quick money at the county market while the grain is still growing.

This year, as every year, I will put my largest piece of land—thirty mu—into the wheat-maize rotation. My winter wheat went into the ground last autumn after a light rotary tillage, and now that the green-up has come, I will top-dress it with urea and irrigate it four times before harvest in early June: at green-up, jointing, heading, and grain-filling. I have seen too many farmers lose their wheat to fusarium or aphids, so I will spray three times to keep it clean. I expect about 480 jin per mu—not the highest, but steady. As soon as the wheat is cut, I will plant my summer maize. Time is short in June; I will not waste a day ploughing. I will seed the hybrid maize directly into the wheat stubble with no-tillage and fertilize it well, because hybrid seed is expensive and I must get my money back. Three irrigations and two pesticide sprays should carry it to a harvest around 520 jin per mu, God willing and the well pump holding out.

I will keep eight mu for cotton. Cotton is hard work and thirsty work, but when the lint price is good, it pays better than grain. I will deep-plough that land in spring and plant an improved variety I know from experience. Cotton must be watched like a child: four irrigations through the summer and five pesticide sprays for bollworm and mites. If I tend it right, I should pick around 300 jin of seed cotton per mu by autumn.

The remaining four mu I will plant with hybrid cucumber in spring. Cucumber needs money up front for seed and fertilizer, but it ripens fast. I will work that plot with rotary tillage, give it heavy manure and fertilizer—more than the grain crops—and water it eight times because it wilts faster than a child cries. I will spray five times to keep downy mildew off the leaves. If the market holds, I hope to haul about 3,500 jin per mu to sell before the summer heat peaks.

I do not have book learning, but I have a well that has never run dry and hands that know when a leaf is hungry or sick. I will not chase miracles. I will do what the land, the weather, and my own back tell me to do.
